prompt: What is a 'phase' in materials science?
options: Any small part of a sample
A region uniform in composition, structure, and properties
A layer of paint on the surface
correctAnswer: A region uniform in composition, structure, and properties
explanation: A phase is internally uniform. Liquid water and ice are different phases. So are α-Fe (BCC, ferrite) and γ-Fe (FCC, austenite) — same atoms, different structure, different properties.

prompt: The Gibbs phase rule for a system at variable temperature and pressure is:
explanation: Degrees of freedom F = components C − phases P + 2, where the 2 counts T and P. A pure substance (C=1) with one phase has F=2 (an area in T-P space); two phases coexist along a curve (F=1); three phases coexist only at a single triple point (F=0).

prompt: At the triple point of water (273.16 K, 611.7 Pa):
options: Solid, liquid, and gas coexist in equilibrium
correctAnswer: Solid, liquid, and gas coexist in equilibrium
explanation: The triple point is the unique combination of T and P at which three phases of a pure substance coexist. By the Gibbs phase rule it is a single point (F = 1 − 3 + 2 = 0). The water triple point was used to define the kelvin until SI was redefined in 2019.

prompt: Above the _____ point, no distinction exists between liquid and gas, and the substance becomes a supercritical fluid.
explanation: The liquid-gas phase boundary terminates at the critical point. Beyond it, the two phases merge continuously and the substance is a supercritical fluid — used industrially as a tunable solvent (e.g. supercritical CO₂ for decaffeinating coffee). For water, T_c ≈ 647 K, P_c ≈ 22 MPa.

prompt: Match each Fe phase to its description:
explanation: Pure iron has α (BCC) at low T, transforms to γ (FCC) at 912 °C, then to δ (BCC) at 1394 °C, and melts at 1538 °C. Each phase has different solubility for carbon — the heart of why steel is heat-treatable.

prompt: What is special about a eutectic composition in a binary alloy?
options: It melts over a wide temperature range
It melts at a single temperature, lower than either pure component
correctAnswer: It melts at a single temperature, lower than either pure component
explanation: The eutectic composition is the lowest-melting liquid in the system. It freezes (and melts) at a single sharp temperature — the eutectic temperature — without an intermediate slush range. This is why it is so useful for soldering: a clean, predictable melt and freeze.

prompt: The eutectic temperature of the lead-tin system is approximately:
explanation: Pb-Sn eutectic is at ~62 % Sn, 183 °C — far below the melting points of pure Pb (327 °C) and pure Sn (232 °C). This eutectic is the reason traditional 60/40 solder works so cleanly: it melts and resolidifies at a single, low temperature.

prompt: Which line on a phase diagram represents the temperature above which all material is liquid?
explanation: The liquidus separates all-liquid from a two-phase mush of solid + liquid. The solidus separates the mush from all-solid. Between them, only fractions of solid and liquid coexist — exactly what the lever rule quantifies.

prompt: Standard lead-free solder under EU RoHS is typically tin-silver-copper, often known by the abbreviation _____.
explanation: SAC305 (96.5 % Sn, 3 % Ag, 0.5 % Cu) is the most common lead-free electronic solder, melting at ~217 °C. It replaced traditional 60/40 Pb-Sn after the EU RoHS directive in 2006, requiring extensive redesign of reflow profiles and component packaging.

prompt: Match each Pb-Sn alloy composition to its expected microstructure:

pairs.right: Fine lamellar α + β eutectic throughout
Primary α grains in a matrix of α + β eutectic
Primary β grains in a matrix of α + β eutectic

explanation: Microstructure depends on starting composition relative to the eutectic. The two-phase eutectic mixture forms wherever residual liquid hits the eutectic point during cooling. Off-eutectic alloys produce primary grains first, then a eutectic matrix between them.

prompt: A horizontal line drawn at the temperature of interest, terminating on the boundaries of two phases, is called a:
explanation: The tie line connects the compositions of two coexisting phases at the temperature of interest. Its endpoints give the phase compositions; lever-rule lengths along the tie line give the relative amounts of each phase.

prompt: The lever rule essentially expresses:
options: A mass balance — the overall composition is the weighted average of the phase compositions
correctAnswer: A mass balance — the overall composition is the weighted average of the phase compositions
explanation: The lever rule is just mass conservation: if the alloy is C₀ and the two phases are at C_α and C_β, then f_α C_α + f_β C_β = C₀ with f_α + f_β = 1. Solving gives f_α = (C_β − C₀)/(C_β − C_α).

prompt: An alloy of overall composition 30 % B sits in a two-phase region where α has 10 % B and β has 90 % B. What is the mass fraction of α?
explanation: Lever rule: f_α = (C_β − C₀) / (C_β − C_α) = (90 − 30) / (90 − 10) = 60/80 = 0.75. So 75 % of the alloy is the α phase, 25 % is β. The lever rule turns the diagram into a quantitative microstructure prediction.

prompt: Phase diagrams describe equilibrium. Real microstructures in fast-cooled alloys may differ because the system has not reached _____ equilibrium.
explanation: Phase diagrams are equilibrium maps; reaching them requires sufficient time for atoms to diffuse. Rapid cooling can suppress phase transformations entirely (martensite formation in steel, glass formation in oxides and polymers). The diagram tells you the destination; kinetics tells you whether the alloy gets there.

prompt: Match each tie-line concept to its meaning:

pairs.right: Compositions of the two coexisting phases
Mass fractions of the two phases

pairs.left: Position of the alloy composition C₀

explanation: The tie line has three roles. Its endpoints fix the two phase compositions. The alloy composition C₀ is the fulcrum. The lengths from C₀ to each endpoint determine the phase fractions via the lever rule. Together these turn a phase diagram into a precise microstructure predictor.

prompt: Plain-carbon steel is defined as iron with carbon up to a maximum of approximately:
explanation: The boundary between steel and cast iron in the Fe-C diagram is the maximum carbon solubility in austenite at 1147 °C — about 2.1 % C. Above that limit, the alloy is classified as cast iron. The 6.67 % figure is the carbon content of pure cementite (Fe₃C).

prompt: What forms when austenite of eutectoid composition (0.76 % C) is slowly cooled below 727 °C?
options: Pearlite — a fine lamellar mixture of ferrite + cementite
correctAnswer: Pearlite — a fine lamellar mixture of ferrite + cementite
explanation: At the eutectoid point, austenite transforms to a fine lamellar mixture of ferrite and cementite called pearlite. The structure looks like alternating dark and light layers under a microscope and gives diffraction-coloured iridescence — hence the name.

prompt: Why does fast quenching of austenitic steel produce martensite instead of pearlite?
options: Carbon does not have time to diffuse out of the FCC lattice, so the structure shears into a strained, supersaturated BCT phase
Martensite is the equilibrium product at low temperature
correctAnswer: Carbon does not have time to diffuse out of the FCC lattice, so the structure shears into a strained, supersaturated BCT phase
explanation: Equilibrium decomposition into ferrite + cementite requires carbon to diffuse out of the iron lattice. Rapid quenching denies that time. The FCC lattice instead shears diffusionlessly into BCT martensite, with all the carbon trapped interstitially. The result is hard and brittle until tempered.

prompt: After quenching, steel is reheated to 200–600 °C in a step called _____ to recover ductility while retaining most of the hardness.
explanation: Tempering allows controlled precipitation of fine cementite from the supersaturated martensite, reducing brittleness while leaving most of the hardness in place. Quench-and-temper is the universal recipe for tools, blades, gears, and bearings.

prompt: Match each Fe-C phase or product to its key property:

pairs.right: Soft, ductile, magnetic — low C solubility
Very hard, metastable BCT phase from quenching

explanation: Each phase or product contributes a different mechanical character. Plain steels combine ferrite, cementite, and pearlite; heat-treatable steels add tempered martensite. The Fe-C diagram plus quench-and-temper kinetics together explain almost every plain-carbon steel microstructure in industry.

prompt: Which pair of metals forms a complete solid solution at all compositions?
explanation: Cu and Ni satisfy all four Hume-Rothery rules — both FCC, similar atomic size, similar electronegativity, similar valence — and they form a continuous solid solution at every composition. The Cu-Ni system is the textbook example of a 'lens' (isomorphous) phase diagram.

prompt: Which of the following is NOT one of the Hume-Rothery rules for extensive substitutional solid solubility?
explanation: Hume-Rothery's four conditions are similar atomic radii (within ~15 %), same crystal structure, similar electronegativity, and same valence. Electrical conductivity is not part of the rules — it is an emergent property, not a control variable.

prompt: Which compound is the precipitate strengthener in nickel-base superalloys for jet turbine blades?
explanation: Ni₃Al, called the γ' (gamma prime) phase, forms ordered FCC-type precipitates inside an FCC γ matrix. The precipitates are ~50 % of volume in a typical superalloy and obstruct dislocation motion at temperatures over 1000 °C — enabling modern high-bypass jet engines.

prompt: Alloys with five or more principal components in roughly equal proportions, like CrMnFeCoNi, are called _____-entropy alloys.
explanation: High-entropy alloys (HEAs) have configurational entropy so large that the disordered solid solution is stabilised against decomposition into intermetallics. CrMnFeCoNi (the Cantor alloy) is the most studied; it has surprising strength and ductility down to cryogenic temperatures.

prompt: Match each example to its category:

pairs.right: Intermetallic compound used in shape-memory alloys

explanation: The same atoms can sit in completely different structures depending on chemistry and temperature. Disordered solid solutions, ordered superlattices, and intermetallic compounds form a hierarchy of increasing chemical specificity — each producing different mechanical and physical behaviour.
